packs.title: Across the City
packs.promise: Explore Montréal through a mountain view, living collections, markets and island time.

q.s: Make a small architectural study without needing a drawing lesson.
st: Use the free site map or ask reception for an open visitor area with a view of the dome. Stay outside rooms in use for services.
Make a tiny study using a curve for the dome, a vertical line for its height, and two lines for the supporting building. Four written shape descriptions work just as well.
Give the study your own short title, then add one sentence about whether the building feels heavy, light or balanced to you.

q.s: Let one gallery work teach you how to arrange a new scene.
st: In an open gallery, choose an artwork that uses a clear arrangement of shapes. Read its title and artist, then look at where your eye goes first.
Describe the arrangement as three positions: foreground, middle and background, or left, centre and right. The work need not depict a landscape.
Invent a different scene using the same arrangement. Make a small pencil sketch if permitted, or describe it in three sentences.
Name the artwork that prompted you and give your own scene a new title. Keep the two clearly separate.

q.s: Make an observation first, then let a botanical label add to it.
st: After admission, choose a labelled plant reachable from an open visitor path or greenhouse aisle. First describe a visible feature without reading the label.
Read the label. Record the plant’s name and one new detail that it gives you; mark anything it does not say as unknown.
Find a second labelled plant with a contrasting visible feature. Compare them in a tiny two-column note: observation and label information.
Keep the collection entirely in your notes. Leave plants, fallen leaves, seeds, fruit and flowers where they are.

packs.title: Squares & Shore
packs.promise: Read Old Montréal through an indoor sky, a small garden and two waterfront viewpoints.

q.s: Collect two different ways a building meets Place d’Armes.
st: Stand in an open part of the square and compare the buildings along two different sides.
Find one repeated feature—columns, arches, windows or another visible pattern—and one feature that breaks the repetition.
Record where each clue belongs using the building’s name if you know it, or its side of the square and a clear description.
Choose which clue would help a friend recognize this square without seeing a photograph.

q.s: Write a tiny exhibit label that keeps evidence and imagination apart.
st: In an open exhibition included in your ticket, choose a displayed object or archaeological feature with interpretation you can read.
Record its name or description and one fact the museum actually gives. Leave uncertain dates, makers or uses uncertain.
Write your own miniature label: one sentence of supported description, then a clearly marked question you would ask about it.
Add a short imagined possibility only if you label it “my possibility”. Your question may remain unanswered.

q.s: Collect two changes in the port’s story from the roof timeline.
st: Use the signed public roof access and find an open portion of the port-history timeline. Stay outside any cordoned private-event area.
Choose two timeline entries about a change: a new connection, technology, building or way of handling goods. Record each date or period exactly as shown.
For each entry, write what changed in one sentence. Then look out from the roof and name one visible feature that raises a question about the port today.
Link the question to one entry without claiming that today’s view proves the whole historical story. A ship does not need to be present.
